newsitem.title: RUSSIA: General has no regrets about Yeltsin criticism.
newsitem.headline: General has no regrets about Yeltsin criticism.

text.p: Russia's defence minister on Friday condemned a top general's attack on his military policy as similar to the agitation which helped Communists seize power in 1917, but the general defiantly stuck to his guns.

"Let us try to learn from our own history," Defence Minister Igor Sergeyev said in an interview in the Defence Ministry daily newspaper Krasnaya Zvezda (Red Star) referring to a withering statement on military reform from prominent general Lev Rokhlin.

"Let us remember the awful result of Bolshevik agitation in the Russian army in 1917. Everyone knows how it all ended," he said. During World War One, much of Russia's demoralised military backed the successful Bolshevik coup d'etat but then fought a debilitating civil war until the early 1920s.

In an open address to President Boris Yeltsin, Rokhlin, a member of the pro-government Our Home is Russia party and chairman of the parliamentary defence committee, said on Tuesday military reform would finally ruin the armed forces.
Rokhlin, a popular figure in the military, also appealed to army officers to stand up for their rights and to resist government plans to scale down the military.

The Communist-led Russian Popular Patriotic Union, a loose grouping of anti-Yeltsin opposition, gleefully backed Rokhlin's statement and said member parties would use their grassroots network to take his call directly to the barracks.
The defiant general said he stuck to his statement, which may cost him membership of Our Home Is Russia and his seat in the State Duma, the lower house of parliament.
"I regret nothing at all," he told Interfax news agency.

"I agreed to include myself in Our Home Is Russia's party list because I wanted to defend the interests of the armed forces in parliament as I understand them," he said. "If they expel me I am not going to join any other political grouping."
Rokhlin insisted the situation was critical, saying: "Won't it end in mutiny?"
He has denied political motives are behind his move, which some experts have described as an early warning from angry generals alarmed by plans to reform their so far unchallenged domain.
Sergeyev argued that the reform was inevitable.
"By 2001 the army will become completely ineffective, uncontrollable and disarmed if we go on without radical change," the former strategic command chief said.

Since the fall of Soviet communism in 1991 the army has been dogged by chronic cash shortages. Officers often go months without pay and underfed conscripts have been reduced to begging in the streets. Suicide, theft, murder and bullying of young recruits by senior officers have become commonplace.
Yeltsin, outraged by the dramatic decline of the huge but largely ineffective military machine, made Sergeyev minister last month, ordering him to start long-delayed reforms.

Yeltsin has said he wants the armed forces to be cut to 1.2 million troops from about 1.8 million as part of a long-term strategy to transform the ramshackle, conscript-based forces into a leaner, professional fighting machine.
Shrugging off accusations that reforms were being prepared by civilians behind the backs of the military, Sergeyev said his plan had been coordinated with all top officers.
"My report to the president has just a few pages but it incorporates the efforts of many people," he said.
"Before presenting it to the president it has received the support of all deputy ministers, commanders of all branches of the forces and approved by Prime Minister Viktor Chernomyrdin."
Sergeyev urged soldiers to contribute to the reforms and even offered an address -- K-160, 103160 Moscow -- for them to write in with their suggestions.
